title: Redwood Inference x GCP Cloud Marketplace review (SKU structure + technical validation + copy)
topics: SKU / plan structure guidance for SaaS listings (GCP Marketplace)
Technical validation steps: entitlement, provisioning, and webhook handling
Copy compliance and restricted security/compliance claims
Region/residency wording and support contact requirements
summary: GCP Marketplace reviewer walked Redwood through recommended plan/SKU structure for a SaaS subscription listing and flagged copy compliance issues to fix prior to re-submission. Key guidance: keep plans simple (avoid excessive plan permutations), be explicit about what is provisioned on purchase vs what requires org-linking in Redwood Console, and ensure the listing includes clear steps for entitlement activation and support escalation. Reviewer also highlighted disallowed/overbroad compliance claims (e.g., implying HIPAA/FedRAMP) and asked Redwood to tighten data residency language. Next steps: Redwood to revise plan names/descriptions, add a short “purchase -> link org -> activate” section, and submit updated security wording and the technical validation checklist items.
next_steps: Redwood (Soojin) to update GCP listing copy: remove/soften compliance claims, add step-by-step activation instructions, and align plan names with SKU catalog.
Redwood (Ethan) to confirm procurement webhook endpoint behavior (idempotency + retry) and provide a short validation note for the reviewer.
GCP (Priya) to send Redwood the current SaaS listing copy policy link + required fields checklist (support URL, privacy policy, terms URL, and provisioning steps).
Redwood (Talia) to schedule a 30-min follow-up after resubmission to review any remaining validation errors.
transcript:
Meeting title: Redwood Inference x GCP Cloud Marketplace review (SKU structure + technical validation + copy)
Recorded: 2025-01-16 18:00:12 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees:
- Talia Benson (Redwood Inference)
- Soojin Lee (Redwood Inference)
- Ethan Park (Redwood Inference)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Desai (Google Cloud Marketplace)
- Miguel Alvarez (Google Cloud Marketplace)

----

[00:00] Talia Benson: Alright, I think we’re live. Priya, Miguel, thanks for making the time. The goal today is to make sure our GCP Marketplace listing and SKUs are structured correctly, and we’re not missing anything for the technical validation.

[00:14] Priya Desai: Yep, sounds good. Thanks, Talia. I did a first pass on the draft listing and also the plan structure you sent in the portal. There are a couple things we should fix before you resubmit.

[00:26] Soojin Lee: Great. We’re happy to iterate. We’re trying to keep it consistent with AWS, but we know GCP has different constraints.

[00:34] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah and also GCP Marketplace has some… like the way we present SaaS plans is a bit opinionated. We can talk through what will pass review.

[00:43] Talia Benson: Perfect. Maybe start with SKU structure?

[00:47] Priya Desai: Sure. Right now you have, I think, nine plans? Hosted, Dedicated, Private, and then each has three variations for compliance and retention and premium SLA.

[00:58] Soojin Lee: Yeah, we modeled it as base plus add-ons, but the portal kind of pushes us to “plans,” so we made combinations.

[01:06] Priya Desai: Right. The main issue is: too many combinations reads as “pricing matrix” and it becomes hard for customers to choose. For SaaS, we recommend 3 to 5 plans maximum.

[01:18] Naomi Feldman: Is the limitation a strict policy limit or more like a guidance to avoid rejection?

[01:24] Priya Desai: It’s not a hard numeric limit, but if it’s too many, reviewers can flag it as confusing and ask you to simplify. In your case, also, your plan names are very similar, which increases confusion.

[01:38] Talia Benson: Understood. If we keep Hosted, Dedicated, Private as the top-level plans, how do we represent add-ons like compliance packet, longer retention, and premium SLA?

[01:49] Miguel Alvarez: In GCP Marketplace, for SaaS, you typically either bundle the add-ons into higher tiers—like “Enterprise” includes retention and premium support—or you keep add-ons off-marketplace and sell them via order form / direct, but that’s a business decision.

[02:05] Soojin Lee: We do need them to be purchasable through marketplace for procurement reasons. At least compliance and retention come up a lot.

[02:12] Priya Desai: Then the cleanest is probably: make “Hosted API” two plans: “Standard” and “Enterprise.” Enterprise includes the things that are actually toggles—like longer log retention, audit log export, and premium SLA.

[02:28] Naomi Feldman: Just to clarify, our “compliance add-on” isn’t like a product feature that turns on compliance. It’s more like additional controls and documentation plus, in some cases, retention configuration. So we have to be careful.

[02:41] Priya Desai: Exactly, and that’s the other piece: your current copy implies that buying the compliance add-on makes you compliant with HIPAA and ISO and so on.

[02:50] Soojin Lee: Okay, that’s helpful. We’ll fix that language.

[02:53] Talia Benson: On Dedicated and Private, we have reserved capacity and VPC deployment. Is that typically a separate marketplace plan or do you prefer it’s one “Private” plan with custom pricing?

[03:05] Miguel Alvarez: You can do a “contact us” style plan with a starting price and then private offer for the final. But you still need a plan in the listing.

[03:16] Priya Desai: Right. Marketplace needs a public plan structure, even if most enterprise customers convert via private offer. We just need the plan to be accurate.

[03:25] Ethan Park: For “Private,” our deployment is not a GCP VM image. It’s more like: customer purchases, then we entitle and set up a private control plane and connect it to their VPC. So it’s still SaaS, just deployed into their environment.

[03:39] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, that’s still a SaaS listing; it’s just a different provisioning path. You’ll need to explain the steps clearly.

[03:47] Priya Desai: Exactly. Which brings us to technical validation. For SaaS, we validate that after purchase, the buyer can actually activate the product without emailing you for a secret step.

[03:59] Talia Benson: We do have an org linking flow in our Console. After purchase, they click “Manage on Provider” and it routes them to Redwood, and they link the GCP billing account to a Redwood org.

[04:12] Priya Desai: That’s fine. But your listing currently says “Instant access after purchase.” That’s probably going to get flagged if there’s an additional linking step.

[04:21] Soojin Lee: Ah, yep. That’s an AWS phrasing we used. We’ll update to something like “Access after completing org linking in Redwood Console,” and then a short step-by-step.

[04:32] Priya Desai: Yes. And keep it short. Like: 1) Purchase in Marketplace 2) Open Redwood Console 3) Link org 4) You’ll see entitlement active.

[04:44] Ethan Park: On the backend, we ingest the procurement events via webhook. We also do retries and idempotency because sometimes the partner system sends duplicates.

[04:53] Miguel Alvarez: Good. Make sure you have logging around failed webhook validation. We sometimes see partners accept unsigned payloads.

[05:01] Ethan Park: We validate signatures. For GCP it’s the… JWT signed by Google, right? We validate the issuer and audience and the cert chain. We can send a short note.

[05:12] Priya Desai: Great. The validation checklist will ask for: how you verify the event, how you map it to the customer tenant, and how you handle subscription cancellation.

[05:23] Talia Benson: Cancellation is important. We currently have a grace period; if a subscription ends, we set the entitlement to “inactive” and the API keys stop working within, I think, 30 minutes.

[05:34] Soojin Lee: It might be 15 minutes. Ethan?

[05:36] Ethan Park: It’s configured to 15, but in practice if there’s retries or delays it can be a little longer. We can commit to “within one hour” for safety.

[05:47] Priya Desai: That’s fine. Just don’t over-promise a precise number if it varies.

[05:53] Naomi Feldman: On copy compliance, besides the HIPAA thing, what else stood out?

[05:58] Priya Desai: A few phrases: “fully compliant with SOC 2” and “ISO certified.” If you are SOC 2 Type II, you can say “SOC 2 Type II audited” or “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA,” but don’t say “fully compliant” as a blanket statement.

[06:16] Naomi Feldman: Okay.

[06:18] Priya Desai: Also “FedRAMP ready” is a common one. You didn’t say that exactly, but you said “government-grade compliance.” That’s usually flagged.

[06:29] Soojin Lee: Got it. We can remove “government-grade.”

[06:32] Miguel Alvarez: For security claims, focus on controls: encryption at rest and in transit, key management, audit logging, SSO, RBAC. Avoid regulated frameworks unless you have explicit attestations.

[06:46] Soojin Lee: Makes sense.

[06:48] Talia Benson: On data residency, we want to be accurate. Our hosted API runs in specific regions, and customers can choose region. Private deployments are in their VPC so residency is aligned to their VPC region.

[07:03] Priya Desai: That can be okay, but your current wording says “supports EU data residency by default.” That’s too broad. We need: which regions are available, and that the customer must select them.

[07:15] Soojin Lee: We’ll change to “Customers can select region at provisioning; available regions listed in documentation,” and link it.

[07:22] Priya Desai: Good. Links are important, but ensure the link is stable and not behind login.

[07:29] Ethan Park: That’s a good point. Some of our docs require sign-in. We can create a public doc page for Marketplace onboarding.

[07:37] Talia Benson: We’re already doing that for AWS. We can mirror for GCP and include “differences vs AWS.”

[07:43] Priya Desai: Great.

[07:45] Miguel Alvarez: Another thing: the “deployment steps” section. For SaaS you still need it. We often see partners leave it empty and just say “sign up.” But we need at least: purchase, redirect, tenant creation or linking, and confirmation.

[07:59] Soojin Lee: We can write that. Also include screenshots?

[08:02] Priya Desai: Not required, but helpful. Just ensure no customer data in screenshots.

[08:09] Talia Benson: Let’s talk plan naming. We currently have “Redwood Hosted API - Pro,” “Redwood Hosted API - Enterprise,” “Redwood Dedicated - 8xH100,” etc. Does GCP have constraints about including hardware in the plan name?

[08:25] Priya Desai: It’s not forbidden, but it can be misleading. Marketplace customers interpret the plan name as the purchased unit. If Dedicated is “8xH100” but you can change underlying hardware later, that can create confusion.

[08:40] Lauren… sorry, Naomi Feldman: We actually can offer multiple hardware pools. But the plan is really “dedicated capacity.” Hardware is implementation detail.

[08:49] Miguel Alvarez: Right. Then I’d recommend: “Dedicated Capacity” with an included baseline and then talk about configuration and sizing after purchase, or via private offer.

[09:01] Soojin Lee: That’s aligned with our messaging anyway.

[09:03] Priya Desai: And keep the short description focused: “Reserved GPU capacity with SLA-backed throughput” etc.

[09:12] Talia Benson: On pricing display: if most Dedicated/Private deals are private offers, do we need a public price?

[09:19] Priya Desai: For public listing, yes, there needs to be a price. It can be a starting price or a minimal commit. Then you can do private offer for final.

[09:30] Talia Benson: Okay.

[09:31] Ethan Park: On the technical side, our provisioning isn’t automatic infra deployment in GCP. It’s entitlement plus configuration. Will that fail validation?

[09:42] Miguel Alvarez: Not necessarily. The question is: can a user who purchased complete activation with self-serve steps, in a reasonable amount of time, without waiting days for human intervention.

[09:54] Ethan Park: For Hosted, yes, it’s self-serve. For Private, we do require a setup call sometimes, mostly for networking. But we can provide a clear “we will contact you within X business day” kind of flow.

[10:06] Priya Desai: Private / VPC type solutions can be “assisted provisioning.” That’s acceptable, but you must state it in the listing and set expectations.

[10:15] Soojin Lee: Great, we’ll adjust Private plan language accordingly.

[10:18] Priya Desai: Also, in your FAQ you have “refunds available on request.” That’s not really how Marketplace works. Refunds are governed by the Marketplace refund policies. You can link to your internal policy, but don’t contradict GCP’s.

[10:33] Talia Benson: That’s a good catch. We’ll remove that or align it.

[10:36] Naomi Feldman: What about support SLAs wording? Our premium SLA add-on includes a contractual SLA.

[10:43] Priya Desai: You can say “Premium support options available” and “SLA available for eligible plans.” Avoid stating numeric uptime in the listing unless you can guarantee it for all customers on that plan.

[10:56] Soojin Lee: So even “99.9% uptime” might be flagged?

[10:59] Priya Desai: It can pass if it’s accurate and contractually enforced, but reviewers may ask for confirmation. Most partners keep it less specific in the listing and handle details in the contract.

[11:12] Talia Benson: We can keep it as “SLA-backed options” without the number.

[11:15] Miguel Alvarez: That will reduce review back-and-forth.

[11:19] Priya Desai: Switching to required fields: We need a support email, a support URL, privacy policy URL, and terms URL. Your draft has “contact sales” but not the actual URLs.

[11:34] Soojin Lee: Okay. We can add those. Terms are on our site, privacy too.

[11:38] Talia Benson: For support email, can we use marketplace-support@redwoodinference.com? Or do you prefer a specific alias?

[11:44] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[11:46] Ethan Park: On the procurement event flow, do you need us to show evidence in the portal? Like screenshots of the entitlement activation?

[11:54] Miguel Alvarez: Not usually. But we might ask you to run through a purchase in a test environment and demonstrate that the flow works. That’s part of partner engineering validation.

[12:07] Priya Desai: Yeah. If you get a validation error, the portal will show something like “Cannot verify provisioning steps.” That’s typically resolved by adding the steps and ensuring “Manage on Provider” link works.

[12:21] Talia Benson: Understood.

[12:22] Soojin Lee: Can you clarify the “Manage on Provider” requirement? We currently route to a generic landing page that prompts login.

[12:30] Priya Desai: It should go to a page that clearly indicates what to do for marketplace buyers. If it’s a generic login, that’s not great. Ideally you detect marketplace context or at least have instructions.

[12:43] Ethan Park: We can include a param in the redirect and show a “Marketplace activation” page, then login, then the wizard.

[12:50] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[12:52] Miguel Alvarez: A common pattern is: “If you already have a tenant, link; if not, create.” Make sure you handle multiple accounts.

[13:02] Talia Benson: We’ve seen that in AWS too—customers have multiple cloud billing accounts. We’re adding an org linking UI to avoid linking to wrong org.

[13:11] Priya Desai: Great. If you can add a line like “Ensure you are logged into the correct Redwood organization,” that helps.

[13:20] Naomi Feldman: Back to compliance language: We can say “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA,” “encryption at rest and in transit,” “customer data is not used to train models” (for our platform), etc. Is that okay?

[13:35] Priya Desai: “Not used to train” is okay if it’s true and covered in your privacy policy/terms. Reviewers sometimes ask you to reference a doc.

[13:43] Soojin Lee: We can link to a data processing addendum page.

[13:47] Priya Desai: Great.

[13:49] Ethan Park: Are there any constraints about mentioning “VPC” in the listing for Private? Like is “VPC” okay or do we need to say “VPC network” for GCP?

[13:58] Miguel Alvarez: People say “VPC” all the time, it’s fine. If you want to be precise, you can say “customer-managed VPC network” or “VPC” and then clarify in docs.

[14:09] Talia Benson: Okay.

[14:10] Priya Desai: Another note: Your listing currently references “GKE add-on.” But from what I understand, you’re not actually distributing a GKE add-on artifact.

[14:21] Ethan Park: Correct. That might have been a copy artifact. We don’t have a GKE add-on. We integrate via network/private endpoints.

[14:28] Soojin Lee: We’ll remove that.

[14:30] Priya Desai: Yeah, remove to avoid confusion.

[14:33] Talia Benson: Any other copy compliance gotchas we should watch for?

[14:38] Priya Desai: Avoid “guaranteed cost savings,” avoid benchmarking claims without context like “fastest” unless you have a cited benchmark. And avoid naming competitors negatively.

[14:50] Soojin Lee: We did include “faster than open-source serving stacks” or something like that.

[14:54] Priya Desai: That one is borderline. If you say “optimized for low latency and throughput” it’s safer.

[15:01] Miguel Alvarez: We’re not trying to water it down, but you’ll pass review faster with less absolute language.

[15:07] Soojin Lee: Understood.

[15:09] Ethan Park: About metering. For Hosted API we have per-token usage. For Dedicated it’s more like a monthly commit. For Marketplace, do we have to implement usage metering via GCP’s metering API?

[15:25] Miguel Alvarez: For SaaS listings you generally integrate with the procurement API, and your billing can be based on the plan price. If you want usage-based charges, that’s a separate structure and it gets more complex.

[15:38] Talia Benson: So for simplicity, we can make Hosted a commitment-based plan rather than true usage-based in GCP?

[15:46] Priya Desai: That’s typically what partners do, yes. Like “Included credits” or “up to X” and overages handled outside. But again that’s your business model.

[15:59] Soojin Lee: We want to keep it aligned with internal billing. We can sell “committed spend” through Marketplace that maps to our internal token meters.

[16:08] Ethan Park: Technically, we can entitle a monthly credit amount and then enforce within Redwood.

[16:13] Miguel Alvarez: Exactly. And that’s much easier for Marketplace.

[16:18] Naomi Feldman: If we do a credit-based plan, do we need to specify exactly how many tokens that equals?

[16:24] Priya Desai: You can describe it in dollar credits. If you describe tokens, it gets tricky because token pricing changes per model. Better: “$X/month of usage,” and link to pricing page.

[16:36] Soojin Lee: That aligns with what we’re doing on AWS too.

[16:39] Talia Benson: Okay, so plan structure proposal: Hosted Standard and Hosted Enterprise (credit-based). Dedicated (starting at some baseline monthly). Private (assisted provisioning, private offer). That’s four.

[16:55] Priya Desai: That sounds more reasonable.

[16:58] Miguel Alvarez: Plus you can include “Compliance & Audit Add-on” as included in Enterprise, rather than a separate plan.

[17:05] Naomi Feldman: We just need to make sure Enterprise doesn’t imply “regulated compliance,” but rather “enterprise security controls.”

[17:12] Priya Desai: Exactly.

[17:14] Soojin Lee: For the portal, do you want the plan short descriptions under 250 chars? We saw some UI truncation.

[17:22] Priya Desai: Yes, keep them concise. Long description can be longer.

[17:28] Talia Benson: On technical validation timeline, once we resubmit, how long does review take?

[17:35] Priya Desai: Typically 5 to 10 business days for initial review, depending on queue. If there are issues, it can go back and forth.

[17:45] Talia Benson: Okay.

[17:46] Ethan Park: If we change plan IDs, does it break anything on your side?

[17:50] Miguel Alvarez: If you already have active subscribers, yes it matters. But I assume you haven’t launched yet.

[17:55] Talia Benson: Correct, no active GCP Marketplace customers yet.

[17:58] Priya Desai: Then it’s fine.

[18:00] Soojin Lee: We also have internal requirement: SKU naming consistency across AWS and GCP. But we can make GCP plan names a bit simpler while keeping internal mapping.

[18:10] Priya Desai: That’s fine. Customers only see what’s in the listing.

[18:15] Naomi Feldman: One question: Can we attach a security packet PDF as an artifact in the listing?

[18:21] Priya Desai: You can include security overview content on your website and link it. Attachments are possible but it depends. If the packet includes confidential audit reports, we don’t want that publicly accessible.

[18:33] Naomi Feldman: Understood. Our SOC 2 report is NDA-only.

[18:36] Miguel Alvarez: For NDA-only, include “available upon request” language and a contact.

[18:41] Talia Benson: Great.

[18:44] Priya Desai: Another point: Your “What happens to data” section implies you store prompts for 30 days “for all customers.” But then elsewhere you say customers can configure retention.

[18:57] Soojin Lee: Yes. Standard has default retention, Enterprise can have shorter retention and export options.

[19:04] Priya Desai: Then you need consistent language: “Default retention is X for Standard; configurable for Enterprise.” And be careful saying “0 retention” unless you truly can.

[19:16] Ethan Park: We can reduce retention but we still keep some operational logs for security and billing.

[19:21] Naomi Feldman: Exactly, we have audit logs which are different than prompt content.

[19:26] Priya Desai: Great, then specify categories: “request logs,” “audit logs,” “billing events,” etc. That clarity helps review.

[19:36] Soojin Lee: Got it.

[19:38] Miguel Alvarez: Also, if you mention encryption keys, don’t imply customers always bring their own KMS key unless it’s actually supported in the plan.

[19:47] Naomi Feldman: We support KMS integration for Private, and for Hosted we use cloud-managed keys. We should say that.

[19:54] Priya Desai: Yes.

[19:55] Talia Benson: What about the “auditable logging” claim? We have audit events for admin actions and API usage metrics. Is it okay to say “audit logs available”?

[20:05] Priya Desai: That’s fine. Avoid “immutable logs” unless you provide immutability guarantees.

[20:12] Ethan Park: We do have append-only log storage internally but I wouldn’t call it immutable.

[20:16] Soojin Lee: We won’t.

[20:18] Talia Benson: Okay. Switching gears—what are the most common reasons SaaS listings fail validation?

[20:26] Priya Desai: The top two are: unclear provisioning steps, and missing required URLs (terms/privacy/support). And then overly aggressive security/compliance claims.

[20:38] Miguel Alvarez: Also, if “Manage on Provider” link goes to a 404 or requires special IP allowlists. That can fail.

[20:46] Ethan Park: It won’t. It’s a public HTTPS page.

[20:49] Priya Desai: Good.

[20:51] Soojin Lee: Is there a specific wording you prefer for “assisted provisioning” for Private?

[20:58] Priya Desai: Something like: “After purchase, Redwood will contact you within 1 business day to complete private deployment setup.” And also include what info you need from them: VPC details, region, etc.

[21:12] Talia Benson: That’s good. We can list prerequisites.

[21:15] Ethan Park: We’ll keep prerequisites light, but include “network connectivity” and “SSO optional.”

[21:20] Naomi Feldman: Just ensure SSO is described as optional depending on plan.

[21:25] Priya Desai: Exactly.

[21:27] Miguel Alvarez: One more: If you mention “on-prem,” that is not something Marketplace validates on GCP. So if you offer on-prem in general, keep it out of the GCP listing or clarify it’s separate.

[21:39] Soojin Lee: Good point. Our “Private” includes on-prem as an option, but GCP Marketplace should focus on GCP VPC deployment.

[21:47] Talia Benson: We’ll align that.

[21:49] Priya Desai: Great.

[21:52] Talia Benson: Can we talk about the portal error we got last time? It said something like “Plan description does not meet policy.” Do you recall what triggered it?

[22:03] Priya Desai: Yes, it was the phrase “HIPAA compliant” and “ISO certified.” That triggered manual review flags. Also you had “GDPR certified,” which isn’t really a thing.

[22:16] Soojin Lee: Oh, yeah, that’s on us. We’ll remove.

[22:18] Naomi Feldman: We can say “supports GDPR-aligned processing” or “Data processing addendum available.”

[22:25] Priya Desai: That’s better.

[22:27] Miguel Alvarez: If you want to mention GDPR, reference your DPA and privacy policy. Don’t call it a certification.

[22:35] Talia Benson: Great.

[22:37] Ethan Park: For the procurement integration, do you need a specific test account to validate? Like will you do a $0 purchase?

[22:45] Miguel Alvarez: We can do test transactions depending on your setup. Priya can send the instructions. Usually it’s in the partner engineering channel.

[22:54] Priya Desai: Yep, I’ll send you the checklist and the “test purchase” instructions.

[22:58] Talia Benson: Thank you.

[23:00] Soojin Lee: One more question: we want to include keywords for search. Are there restricted keywords? Like “OpenAI compatible” etc.

[23:09] Priya Desai: Avoid trademarked competitor names unless it’s factual interoperability. If you say “OpenAI-compatible API,” that is generally okay if it’s a generic API format, but be careful with the name. “OpenAI API compatible” sometimes is flagged.

[23:24] Soojin Lee: We’ll keep it as “OpenAI-style API” or “drop-in REST API.”

[23:29] Priya Desai: That’s safer.

[23:31] Talia Benson: Cool. Anything else you need from us for this cycle?

[23:36] Priya Desai: Just the updated copy and plan structure, and the required URLs. And your provisioning steps. Once you resubmit, I’ll re-review.

[23:48] Miguel Alvarez: And if you can include a short note in the “technical details” section about entitlement propagation time, that helps set expectation. Like “activation typically within a few minutes.”

[23:58] Ethan Park: That’s reasonable. We usually activate within 1-3 minutes.

[24:02] Soojin Lee: We’ll say “typically within minutes.”

[24:04] Priya Desai: Great.

[24:06] Talia Benson: Let’s recap action items quickly.

[24:09] Talia Benson: Redwood side: Soojin updates the copy, plan names, removes restricted compliance phrasing, adds step-by-step activation and assisted provisioning notes for Private.

[24:20] Soojin Lee: Yep.

[24:21] Talia Benson: Ethan sends a short description of our webhook validation and idempotency behavior and cancellation handling, and we’ll incorporate it in the technical section.

[24:30] Ethan Park: Yep, I can do that today or tomorrow.

[24:33] Talia Benson: Naomi will review the security/compliance language so we don’t overstate.

[24:39] Naomi Feldman: Yes.

[24:40] Talia Benson: Priya, you’ll send us the policy link and required fields checklist plus test purchase instructions.

[24:48] Priya Desai: Correct.

[24:50] Talia Benson: Great.

[24:52] Priya Desai: And just to set expectations—if you resubmit with simpler plans and cleaner claims, it should go smoothly.

[24:59] Soojin Lee: Appreciate it.

[25:01] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, and if you hit any portal validation errors, just forward the text. Often it’s the same handful of issues.

[25:08] Talia Benson: Will do.

[25:10] (brief crosstalk)

[25:12] Soojin Lee: Priya, one last tiny thing—do you care if we use “Dedicated” vs “Reserved capacity” in the plan name?

[25:19] Priya Desai: “Reserved capacity” is clearer. “Dedicated” can be interpreted as single-tenant, which you might or might not guarantee. If it is single-tenant, you can say “isolated capacity,” but again be accurate.

[25:34] Soojin Lee: Great point. We do provide isolated GPU pools for Dedicated. We’ll say “Reserved, isolated capacity.”

[25:41] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[25:43] Talia Benson: Okay, thanks everyone. We’ll follow up with the updated submission.

[25:48] Priya Desai: Sounds good.

[25:49] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks.

[25:50] Call ends.

----
Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Summary:
- Reviewer recommended reducing plan combinations and bundling add-ons into higher tiers.
- Listing must clearly explain post-purchase org linking/activation (not “instant access”).
- Remove/avoid broad compliance claims; focus on specific controls and NDA-only attestations.
- Add required URLs (terms, privacy, support) and clarify residency/retention statements.

Questions captured:
- Can add-ons be separate plans? (Prefer bundling into higher tiers)
- Is assisted provisioning acceptable for Private/VPC? (Yes, if disclosed and expectations set)
- Can usage metering be token-based? (Prefer credit/commit-based plan pricing for simplicity)

Action items:
- Soojin: Revise GCP listing copy + plan names; add activation steps; remove restricted claims.
- Ethan: Provide webhook validation/idempotency + cancellation/entitlement propagation note.
- Priya: Send SaaS listing policy links + required fields checklist + test purchase instructions.
